blocks.text: Bronze Age political maps contained separate kingdoms, but resource networks already crossed their borders. Copper, tin, timber and grain were not concentrated in one place. Cities and palaces depended on continuing cooperation among mines, carriers, merchants and ports. Distant conditions affected local capabilities.

Exchange also needed political support. Diplomacy, gifts and mutual recognition could sustain relations among powers. A modest political center could exert influence far beyond its territory by occupying an important route.

blocks.caption: Mycenaean Greece · Context illustration; historical interpretation is in the text.

blocks.text: These connections increased capabilities while transmitting difficulties. Disrupted supplies and transport placed pressure on dependent organizations, allowing local problems to spread. Bronze Age breakdown needs to be understood within this vulnerability, rather than reduced to one cause explaining every region.

Breakdown did not mean that every civilization disappeared simultaneously. Loss, adaptation and inheritance differed among regions, cities and institutions. Political termination, network reorganization and continuing social life must be distinguished to understand how the crisis changed the world.
